title: Krishna Obtains the Celestial Hall Sudharman
story:
Ugrasena sat once more on the throne of Mathura, and around him his people, the Yadavas, had begun to recover from the long fear of Kamsa — Kamsa, his own son, who had seized the throne and thrown his father into prison before Krishna struck him down. Krishna, who had freed the old king from his confinement and placed the crown back upon his head, stood before him as a servant, not a sovereign. The funeral rites for Kamsa and the rest of the slain were done.

Command boldly what else is to be done, Krishna said to him.

There was a difficulty in the way, and Krishna named it openly. The curse of Yayati, he told the king, has pronounced our race unworthy of dominion. Long ago Yayati's son Yadu refused to take his father's old age upon himself, and for that refusal his descendants were denied the right to rule. The Yadavas could hold their assemblies and their court only because they did not do so in their own name. But with me for your servant, Krishna said, you may issue your orders to the gods themselves. How should kings disobey them?

So he set about proving it. There was a hall in the heavens, the splendid Sudharman — a court of unearthly beauty that belonged to Indra, the king of the gods. Krishna turned to Vayu, the god of wind, and gave him an errand. Go to Indra, he said, and ask him to lay aside his pomp and give up his splendid hall Sudharman to Ugrasena.

Vayu carried the request to the king of the gods, and the answer came back without hesitation. Indra laid aside his pomp and gave up the hall at once. The celestial court that had belonged to the lord of heaven passed into the keeping of the Yadava chiefs, who from that day held their assemblies beneath a roof of jewels that no mortal builder had raised.

It was a strange thing to ask for, and stranger still to receive. Krishna did not demand victory in battle, nor wealth, nor a wider kingdom. He asked for a place — a hall where the Yadavas, whom the curse of Yayati had barred from dominion, could sit and hold their counsel with the dignity of kings. And Indra, who had once anointed Krishna by the name Upendra and had sent the golden seat for his consecration, gave it up without a word of refusal.

The curse had not been lifted; the Yadavas still could not claim a crown in their own right. But beneath the jeweled ceiling of Sudharman they gathered as though they could — and the gods, beginning with the one who had been asked to give up his own splendor, did not dispute it.
reflection: The gift Krishna seeks is not power but a place to stand with dignity. Barred by Yayati's curse from dominion, the Yadavas can hold a court only because Krishna, serving them, commands the gods on their behalf. Indra's instant surrender of Sudharman is the measure of that service: even the lord of heaven lays aside his pomp when asked in Ugrasena's name.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha places the hall Sudharman later, among the splendors Krishna brings to Dwaraka; the Vishnu Purana tells it here, for Ugrasena's court at Mathura.
hero_scene: The celestial hall Sudharman descending into the keeping of the Yadava chiefs, its jeweled columns and golden ceiling shining as Indra lays aside his pomp and yields the splendid court.
visual_elements: Ugrasena on the throne of Mathura
Krishna standing as a servant before him
Vayu carrying the request to Indra
the hall Sudharman of jeweled splendor
the Yadava chiefs gathering beneath it
